reels.title: The cake that came out wrong

beats.say: What if your data job finished perfectly, every light green, and still handed you the wrong numbers?

show.sub: A job can succeed and publish bad data

beats.say: Picture a bakery. The oven timer beeps and the cake comes out on time. But someone swapped sugar for salt. Nothing broke. The cake is just wrong, and customers eat it.
Data works the same way. A job can finish without errors while a column went empty, a file arrived twice, or a whole city went missing. A crash is loud. These failures are silent.
So we taste the cake in five ways. Is it fresh? Is there enough? Is the shape right? Do the values make sense? And who eats it if it is bad?

show.title: Five ways to taste the data

check.q: Why are silent data failures more dangerous than crashes?
opts: They are slower to fix once found
The job reports success, so nobody looks and wrong data gets used
They cost more compute
They only affect small tables
check.why: A crash gets noticed and paged. A job that succeeds with wrong data raises no alarm, so people trust and act on bad numbers.

work: List your three most important tables and ask what wrong but successful output would look like.
Check whether any pipeline today relies only on job success as its health signal.

reels.title: Five checks for data that lies

beats.say: Meridian's job ran green, yet twelve percent of trips vanished. How do you catch a failure that never fails?
You check five things. Freshness: is the newest event timestamp under two hours old? Volume: is today's row count inside the band expected for this weekday?
Schema: do columns, types and nullability match the contract? Distribution: is the null rate of driver id under one percent, and has no city's share moved by more than twenty percent?
Lineage: if this table breaks, which dashboards and owners are hit? Each check runs automatically, and the alert goes to someone who can act.

check.q: Which check best catches one city's data silently disappearing?
opts: Freshness on the newest timestamp
Schema check on column types
Distribution check on each city's share
Lineage list of dashboards
check.why: Data is still fresh and the shape is unchanged. Only a per-city share check shows that one slice has shrunk.

work: Pick one table and write one concrete check for each of the five dimensions.
Make sure each alert names an owner who can act, not a shared inbox.

reels.title: How green jobs publish wrong data

beats.say: Why did a renamed column drop twelve percent of trips while every task stayed green?

The app team renamed fare amount to fare. Permissive schema handling filled the old column with nulls. Then a filter on fare amount above zero silently threw those rows away. A schema check or a null-rate check would have stopped it at ingest.

A file sent twice doubled one day's revenue. A volume check catches it, since rows jump far above the weekday band. A missing city is harder. Totals dipped four percent, which looks like normal noise. Only a per-city share check sees it.
The gotcha: a check on totals alone hides a partial loss. Check slices like city and weekday, not just the overall number.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Green tasks do not mean good data
Check slices, not only the total

check.q: Totals dipped 4%, within normal variation, yet one city stopped sending. What would have caught it?
opts: A wider total row count band
A per-city share check
A faster job schedule
More retries on the ingest task
check.why: The loss was too small to stand out in the total. Comparing each city's share to its usual share exposes the missing slice.

work: Add a null-rate check on columns your filters depend on.
Add a deduplication or duplicate-load check on daily file ingests.
Track row counts per key slice, such as city, not only overall.

reels.title: Spending check budget wisely

beats.say: You could check everything, everywhere. Should you?

show.sub: More checks is not more reliable

beats.say: No. Every check costs compute and, worse, attention. Too many noisy alerts and people mute them, and then the real one gets missed.
Put checks where bad data is cheapest to stop: schema and freshness at ingest, volume and distribution before publish. Block the publish on critical tables, warn on the rest.

Use lineage to decide. Tables with many downstream dashboards get strict, blocking checks, and alerts route to the owner. Low impact tables get a warning. Tune bands by weekday, or normal seasonality will page you falsely.

show.title: Spend by blast radius
items: Use weekday bands to avoid false pages

check.q: Which approach best balances reliability and alert fatigue?
opts: Block every pipeline on every check
Strict blocking checks on high-impact tables, warnings on low-impact ones
Only check the final dashboard
Disable checks that ever alert falsely
check.why: Lineage shows the blast radius. Strict checks where many consumers depend, and warnings elsewhere, keep alerts meaningful and trusted.

work: Rank your tables by downstream consumers using lineage and set check strictness accordingly.
Review alert history and retire or retune checks that were ignored repeatedly.
Use weekday-aware volume bands instead of one flat threshold.

reels.title: Three ways to trust a pipeline

beats.say: How do you know a car factory works before a single customer drives away?

First, you test each machine alone, feeding it a few hand-picked parts. If the paint robot cannot paint three test doors, it never joins the line. That is a unit test: small, fast, and run on every change.
Second, an inspector stands at the belt and checks every car that rolls past. Wrong colour? Missing wheel? Stop the line. That is a data test, and it runs all the time, in production.

chip.text: Data test: every run, in production

beats.say: Third, before a new model launches, you build one whole car from a small kit and compare it with the blueprint. That is an integration test.

check.q: An inspector checks every car on the live belt. Which test layer is that?
opts: Unit test
Data test
Integration test
check.why: Data tests check the real data every time it is produced, in production. Unit tests use hand-made inputs, and integration tests run a whole pipeline on a fixed dataset.

work: List which of your pipelines have none of the three layers.
Name one check you do by eye today and write it as an automatic test.

reels.title: Unit testing a Spark job

beats.say: How do you test a Spark job without a cluster, a cloud account, or a ten minute wait?

You write each transformation as a function. It takes a DataFrame in and hands a DataFrame back. Reading and writing stay at the edges of the job. Now the logic never needs a real source, so it can be tested alone.

In the test, you build three rows by hand: two completed trips and one cancelled. Run the function on a local Spark with one thread. Expect Bangalore one, Hyderabad one. If someone drops the status filter, Bangalore shows two, and the test fails in seconds.
Anything external, like an API, gets replaced by a mock. All of this runs in CI on every change.

show.sub: Runs in CI on every change

check.q: Why must reading and writing be kept at the edges of a job?
opts: Spark requires it
So the transformation can be tested with hand-built DataFrames
It makes the job run faster
check.why: When logic is a function from DataFrame to DataFrame, a test can feed it small hand-written data and needs no real source or sink.

work: Refactor one job so the transformation is a pure function of DataFrames.
Write one test with three rows that would fail if your key filter were removed.

reels.title: Data tests and integration tests

beats.say: Your code passed every test, yet tonight's table has duplicate trip ids. How?

Because unit tests only see the data you invented. Data tests check the real data on every run: keys unique and not null, status inside an allowed list, every city id present in the city dimension, row count within a band.

show.title: Data tests, every run
items: Foreign keys exist in the dimension

beats.say: dbt tests and Great Expectations both do this, inside the pipeline in production.

Integration tests are different. Before release, CI runs the whole pipeline on a small fixed dataset, perhaps with real Postgres and Kafka in containers, and compares the output with a known answer. That catches broken wiring between steps.

check.q: Which layer catches duplicate keys in tonight's real production data?
opts: Unit tests
Data tests
Integration tests on a fixed dataset
check.why: Only data tests run on the real data each time it is produced. Unit and integration tests use inputs you chose in advance.

work: Add unique and not null tests on the primary key of your top three tables.
Create a fixed sample dataset and expected output for one end to end CI run.

reels.title: Why green tests still ship bad data

beats.say: Why can a fully green test suite still ship bad data?
Mocks drift. If a mock returns what the real API used to return, your test passes while production breaks. Keep a few integration tests with real services to catch that.
Data tests have a timing trap. If they run after the table is published, consumers already read the bad rows. Run them on a staging table, and promote only when they pass.

Count bands cause trouble too. Set them too tight and weekends trigger false alarms, so people ignore the alerts. Base the band on the same weekday in past weeks. And make your fixtures include ugly rows: nulls, duplicates, late events.

check.q: Data tests run after the table is already published. What is the main risk?
opts: Tests run too slowly
Consumers may read bad rows before the failure is seen
The tests cannot read the table
check.why: A check after publishing only detects damage already done. Testing a staging table and promoting on success stops bad rows reaching consumers.

work: Move your key data tests to run on staging before the swap to live.
Review your row count bands against weekday and weekend history.
Add one real-service integration test for each mocked dependency.

reels.title: Spending your test budget

beats.say: You have a limited test budget. Where do you spend it?
Unit tests are cheapest, so cover business logic heavily there. They cost seconds and no cloud money. Integration tests cost minutes and containers, so keep them few, on the critical paths.
Data tests cost real compute, because each one scans a table. On a billion row table, test only the new partition, and run the full scan weekly.

Give each test a severity. Block the pipeline for a duplicate key in a payments table. Only warn for small drift in a clickstream count. Blocking on everything makes the team disable tests. Warning on everything protects nothing.

show.title: Severity decides
items: Too strict means tests get disabled

check.q: A daily full-table scan test on a billion row table is too costly. What is the best change?
opts: Delete the test
Test only the new partition daily and run the full scan weekly
Replace it with a unit test
check.why: Partition-scoped checks keep daily cost low while the weekly full scan still catches older problems. Deleting loses protection, and unit tests do not see real data.

work: Assign block or warn severity to every data test, based on downstream impact.
Scope daily data tests to the latest partition and schedule full scans weekly.

reels.title: The supplier who changed the flour

beats.say: Imagine your bakery buys flour from a supplier. One day, without a word, they switch to a different flour. How would you know before the bread fails?
A written order slip fixes this. It says what you get, who is responsible, and how much warning you get before anything changes.

show.title: The order slip says
items: How much warning before a change

beats.say: A data contract is that slip. The team producing data promises its shape and meaning. The teams using it can rely on that promise.
And if the supplier wants to change the flour, they must give notice first. Nobody finds out from a ruined loaf.

show.text: Notice first, not a ruined loaf
show.sub: Changes are announced before they ship

check.q: What is the main purpose of a data contract?
opts: To make data load faster
To make the dependency between producers and consumers explicit
To store a backup of the data
check.why: A contract writes down what the producer promises and who depends on it, so changes are not made blindly.

work: List the three tables your team depends on most and who owns each.
Ask one upstream owner how they would warn you about a change today.

reels.title: What a contract actually says

beats.say: A contract is just a file. What does it actually say, and why does each line matter?

show.title: trip_events contract
show.text:
contract: trip_events
version: 2.1.0
owner: rides-app-team
consumers: [data-platform, pricing]

beats.say: It names an owner and a version, like two point one point zero. It also lists consumers, so everyone knows who gets hurt by a change.
The schema lists each field: its type, whether it can be empty, and allowed values. Event type, for example, can only be requested, accepted, started, completed, or cancelled.

show.title: Schema rules per field
items: Type, such as string or decimal

beats.say: Quality rules add numbers. Data must arrive within fifteen minutes of its event time. Hourly volume must sit between sixty and one hundred sixty percent of the same hour last week. A big drop means something broke upstream.

show.title: Volume rule, same hour last week

check.q: Why does the contract list its consumers?
opts: So the producer knows who is affected by a change
So consumers can edit the schema
So data is encrypted for them
check.why: Listing consumers makes the impact of a change visible and tells you who must be given notice.

work: Draft a contract for one table with owner, version, consumers and schema.
Add one freshness rule and one volume rule with real numbers.

reels.title: Enforce it in two places

beats.say: A contract nobody checks is just a document. Where do you enforce it?
First, on the producer side, in CI. That is the automated check that runs on every pull request. If the change renames or removes a field, the build fails before anything ships.
Second, on the consumer side, at ingestion. Every batch is checked against the contract. A bad batch is quarantined, meaning set aside, and the producer's owner gets an alert.
Two layers matter because the first can be missed. In the earlier incident, a renamed column cost twelve percent of the data. The second check would have stopped it before any dashboard.

show.sub: Layer two catches what layer one misses

check.q: Why enforce a contract at both CI and ingestion?
opts: Ingestion checks are faster than CI
If a breaking change slips past CI, ingestion still stops it
CI checks only the data volume
check.why: CI can be bypassed or miss a case. Ingestion validation is the safety net before bad data reaches consumers.

work: Add a schema compatibility step to the producer's pull request pipeline.
Make ingestion quarantine failing batches instead of loading them.

reels.title: When the schema passes but the data lies

beats.say: Your schema check passes, yet the numbers are wrong. How?

Because meaning can change without shape changing. Fare amount is rupees excluding tip, set only on completed trips. If someone starts including tip, the type is still decimal, so a schema check sees nothing.

That is why changing meaning counts as breaking, and needs a new major version and thirty days' notice. Human review catches what a machine cannot. Volume and freshness rules catch silent outages, like a feed that stops or halves.

show.title: What catches what
items: Schema check: renames and type changes
Volume and freshness rules: silent outages

beats.say: Also watch timestamps. Event time comes from the device, so a wrong phone clock can look late or early. Quarantine rather than dropping, so you can replay good data once fixed.

check.q: fare_amount starts including tip. The type stays decimal. What happens?
opts: The schema check fails the batch
A schema check passes, so only review, notice rules or value checks can catch it
The freshness rule fails
check.why: Meaning changes do not alter the type, so schema validation passes. That is why meaning changes are defined as breaking and need review.

work: Write a description of units and meaning on every contract field.
Add value-range checks, such as fares within a sane range, beyond schema checks.

reels.title: Where contracts earn their cost

beats.say: Should every dataset get a contract? Probably not.
Contracts cost effort: owners, versioning, CI checks, notice periods. Spend it where many consumers depend on one source, or where errors cost money, like pricing.
Skip them for one-off exploration or a table with a single team on both sides. A chat and a simple test is cheaper.

Thirty days' notice slows producers, so tie it to real consumer lists. Stale lists make notice worthless. Alternatives are schema registries for automatic compatibility, or tests downstream, which catch problems later but need no producer buy-in.

show.title: Trade-offs
items: Downstream tests: later, no buy-in needed

check.q: Where is a full data contract most worth its cost?
opts: A scratch table used by one analyst
A shared event feed used by pricing and other teams
A temporary file deleted tomorrow
check.why: Contract effort pays off when many consumers depend on one producer and errors are costly.

work: Rank your sources by consumer count and cost of error, and contract only the top few.
Keep the consumer list generated from lineage, not a manual document.

reels.title: A dashboard for your data

beats.say: Your car can pass inspection and still break down next week. How would you know?

show.sub: Rules only catch what you already know

beats.say: Inspection is like a test. It checks rules you already know. A dashboard watches things over time: temperature, fuel, speed. When a number drifts, you notice before the engine dies.
Data pipelines work the same way. Each night we write down simple numbers: how fresh the table is, how many rows arrived, how many blanks. Kept in a table, they become a history.
Now a sudden drop from one million rows to ten thousand stands out. That is observability: noticing change nobody wrote a rule for.

check.q: What does observability add that a fixed test does not?
opts: It notices unexpected change by watching numbers over time
It makes the pipeline run faster
It replaces the need for any tests
check.why: Tests check rules you already thought of. Observability tracks metrics over time so surprises show up even without a specific rule.

work: List the five most important tables you own.
For each, write down what a normal night looks like in rows and freshness.
Ask who would notice first if one silently shrank.

reels.title: What to record and how to flag it

beats.say: What exactly do you record about a table every night?

show.text: What do you record per load?

beats.say: For each load, store freshness lag, row count, null rate of key columns, distinct counts, and a hash of the schema. A hash is a short fingerprint, so any column change alters it. For each job, store duration, retries and cost.
Put these in a table. Then compare today with history. A simple rule: flag a row count more than three standard deviations from the mean of the last seven days.
Say the mean is one million rows, with a spread of fifty thousand. Anything below eight hundred and fifty thousand is flagged. Four hundred thousand rows? Alert.

check.q: Mean is 1,000,000 and standard deviation is 50,000. Which count is flagged by the three-sigma rule?
check.why: The lower limit is 1,000,000 minus 150,000, which is 850,000. Only 820,000 falls below it.

work: Create a metrics table with row count, null rate and schema hash per load.
Backfill seven days from existing partitions.
Run the three-sigma query and see what it would have flagged last month.

reels.title: Why anomaly alerts cry wolf

beats.say: Why does your anomaly alert fire every Monday?

show.text: Why does it fire every Monday?

beats.say: Because weekends are quiet. Compare Monday with Sunday and it looks like a collapse. Fix it by comparing each day with the same weekday, for example the last four Mondays.

show.title: Compare like with like
items: looks like a spike vs Sun

beats.say: Also demand enough history. With two days of data, the spread is meaningless, so every wobble alerts. Wait for a minimum, say four weeks of same-weekday points, before paging anyone.
And watch the noise. An alert that fires daily and is ignored is worse than none, because people stop reading the one that matters.

check.q: Monday row counts always look high against Sunday. What is the best fix?
opts: Raise the threshold to ten standard deviations
Compare each day with the same weekday in past weeks
Turn off alerts on Mondays
check.why: Same-weekday baselines remove weekly seasonality while keeping sensitivity to real drops.

work: Check whether your anomaly rules use a same-weekday baseline.
Add a minimum-history guard so new tables do not alert for four weeks.
Count alerts fired last month and delete any nobody acted on.

reels.title: Reliability as a number

beats.say: Your stakeholder asks, is the pipeline reliable? What number do you give?
A service-level objective. For example: the trips mart is complete by seven in the morning IST on ninety-nine percent of days. Everyone agrees on it up front.

show.title: Example SLO
show.text:
trips mart complete by 07:00 IST
on 99% of days

beats.say: Then you measure. Ninety-nine percent over thirty days allows about one miss. Two misses means last month was not acceptable, and you can say so with evidence instead of feelings.
The trade-off: every extra nine costs more in redundancy and on-call effort. Pick the target the business needs, not the highest one.

check.q: Why define an SLO such as 99 percent of days by 07:00?
opts: It guarantees no failures will happen
It gives an agreed measure to judge whether a period was acceptable
It removes the need for alerts
check.why: An SLO does not prevent failure. It gives everyone a shared, measurable definition of acceptable reliability.

work: Draft one SLO for your most important mart with the stakeholder.
Report last quarter's actual performance against it.
Decide what happens when the error budget is used up.

reels.title: Blast radius and better alerts

beats.say: A table breaks at three in the morning. What else is now wrong?
Lineage answers that. Airflow and Spark emit OpenLineage events, and a catalog like OpenMetadata joins them into a graph of what feeds what.
Walk the graph downstream and you know which dashboards to mark suspect and which owners to tell, before they find the bad number themselves.
Then make the alert good. Few, routed to an owner, saying what failed, what it affects, with a link to the evidence.

check.q: During an incident, what is lineage mainly used for?
opts: Finding which downstream assets and owners are affected
Speeding up the failed query
Computing the row count mean
check.why: Lineage maps dependencies, so you can see the blast radius and notify the right people.

work: Enable OpenLineage emission from your orchestrator and Spark jobs.
Run a drill: pick a table and list the dashboards it feeds.
Add owner and evidence link fields to every alert.

reels.title: Taste before you serve

beats.say: Would a restaurant serve a brand new recipe to customers without tasting it first?
Data teams do the same. Every change starts as a draft, called a pull request. That is a proposal others can read before anything is real.
Then robots taste it. This is CI, short for continuous integration. It checks spelling, runs small tests, and cooks the dish on a little sample in a side kitchen, not the real one.

show.title: Robots *taste* it in a side kitchen

beats.say: Only after a human approves does it reach the dining room. That step is deployment. And if customers dislike it, you swap back to the old recipe and cook the affected meals again.

check.q: Why does a data team run CI on a sample in a separate place before deploying?
opts: To catch mistakes without touching real production data
To make production run faster
To avoid needing a human reviewer
check.why: CI is the side kitchen. It lets robots test a change safely, so mistakes are found before customers or real tables are affected.

work: Write down the path a change takes from your laptop to production at your company.
Find out where your team tests changes, and whether it is separate from production.
Ask who approves a pull request before it goes live.

reels.title: What CI and deploy actually run

beats.say: A pull request touches fifty dbt models out of two thousand. Do you rebuild all two thousand to test it?

No. CI first runs linting for Python and SQL, then unit tests. Then dbt build runs only the changed models and their descendants, in a temporary CI schema, on a sample of data. Unchanged parents are read from production.
If infrastructure changed, terraform plan shows what would change, without changing it. A reviewer reads it before approving.
After merge, deployment ships new DAG files, new job images, and runs terraform apply. Because the plan was reviewed, the apply holds no surprises, and CI stays fast on a huge project.

check.q: On a large dbt project, how does CI stay fast?
opts: It skips tests for unchanged code and models alike
It builds changed models and descendants, reading unchanged parents from production
It builds everything but on a bigger machine
check.why: Building only changed models and their descendants, with unchanged parents read from production, avoids rebuilding the whole project.

work: Check whether your CI builds only changed dbt models and their descendants.
Make terraform plan output visible on every pull request that touches infrastructure.
Time your CI run and find the slowest step.

reels.title: Why a tested job still dies

beats.say: A job passed every test, then died in production with no error in its own code. Why?

Containers package code and dependencies so CI and production run identically. On Kubernetes a container runs in a pod. The pod declares requests, which the scheduler reserves, and limits, which the container may not exceed.
Exceed the memory limit and the container is killed instantly. A Spark executor holding too much data hits this. Tests on a small sample never showed it, so size memory with realistic volumes.

Rollback has a catch too. Reverting code is easy, but bad data is already written. Rerunning the intervals only fixes it if every job is idempotent, meaning a rerun gives the same result, with no duplicates.

show.title: Safe rollback
items: Works only if jobs are idempotent

check.q: A container exceeds its memory limit. What happens?
opts: It is throttled and slows down
It is killed
Kubernetes raises the limit automatically
check.why: Memory cannot be throttled, so a container over its limit is killed. CPU limits slow a container down instead.

work: Set memory requests and limits from measured peak usage on full-size data.
Test that rerunning a job for the same interval gives identical results.
Alert on killed containers so memory problems are noticed early.

reels.title: What CI cannot promise

beats.say: Should every pipeline get a full production copy for testing? Usually not.
Sampled CI schemas are cheap and fast, but samples miss skew, rare nulls and memory pressure. So add a scheduled test on full-scale data, or data diff checks on the changed models.
Pod per task in Airflow gives isolation and exact resource sizing. The cost is startup time, often tens of seconds, which hurts a tiny task. Group small steps, and keep pods for heavy ones.
Rollback by revert depends on idempotency. Where a job cannot be made idempotent, such as sending emails, add a gate or manual approval before deploy.

show.title: When revert is not enough
items: Revert plus rerun needs idempotent jobs
Emails and payments cannot be undone
Add approval gates for those jobs

check.q: Why is sampled CI alone not enough for a heavy Spark job?
opts: Samples cannot run dbt
Samples miss skew and memory pressure that appear at full scale
Samples always cost more than full runs
check.why: A small sample hides skewed keys and memory pressure, so a job can pass CI and still hit its memory limit in production.

work: Add a scheduled full-scale test for your heaviest pipelines.
Decide which tasks deserve their own pod and which should be grouped.
List jobs that are not idempotent and put a deploy gate in front of them.

reels.title: Burst pipe: handling a data incident

beats.say: A pipe bursts in your building. Do you grab a mop first? No. You turn off the water.
Data problems work the same way. First, stop the spread. Pause the jobs that feed other reports, and put a warning on any dashboard that might be wrong.
Second, tell people. Send a short note: what broke, who is affected, and when you will update them next. Silence makes people guess.
Only then hunt for the cause using evidence, fix it, redo the missing work, and write down what you learned. Blame the system, never a person.

check.q: A report is showing wrong numbers. What should you do first?
opts: Dig through logs to find the cause
Pause downstream jobs and mark the report suspect
Write the postmortem while it is fresh
check.why: Stopping the spread keeps the damage from growing while you investigate. Cause-finding and writing up come later.

work: Write down which dashboards would need a warning if your main table went wrong.
Draft a three-line incident message template: what, who, next update time.

reels.title: The five steps, with real numbers

beats.say: Revenue doubled overnight, and the executive dashboard loads at eight. What do you do first?

Stop the spread. Pause the three jobs that read the table, and flag the dashboard as suspect. That takes two minutes. Then tell people within ten: revenue is doubled since two a.m., finance and marketing are affected, next update at nine.
Find the cause with evidence. Compare row counts per run, read the logs, and see the job started twice at ten past two.
Fix the code, then backfill: rerun only the affected days, not the whole history. Finish with a postmortem of what happened and how to prevent it.

check.q: Why do you backfill only the affected intervals?
opts: It is faster and avoids touching correct data
Postmortems require it
It hides the incident from users
check.why: Targeted reruns save compute and time, and do not risk disturbing days that were already correct.

work: Practice finding root cause by comparing row counts per run in your own pipeline logs.
Make sure your orchestrator can rerun a single date range.

reels.title: Where incident response goes wrong

beats.say: Why did the backfill make things worse? Because the rerun was not safe to repeat.

A backfill replays past intervals. If the job appends, rerunning day five adds rows again. Make jobs idempotent: overwrite that day's partition, so running twice gives the same result. And deploy the fix first, or you recreate the bug.

show.title: Safe backfills
items: Overwrite the partition, do not append

beats.say: Stopping the spread means following lineage. Dashboards are not the end. Exports, emailed reports and model features may already hold bad data. Tell those owners too.
Keep updates on schedule even with no news. And once checks pass, clear the suspect flag so people trust the data again.

show.text: Update on time, then clear the flag
show.sub: Trust is rebuilt by visible follow-through

check.q: Which makes a backfill safe to run twice?
opts: Appending rows with a timestamp
Overwriting the target partition
Running it at night
check.why: Overwriting a partition is idempotent: the same input gives the same result however many times it runs. Appending duplicates data.

work: Check whether each of your jobs overwrites or appends, and fix the append ones.
List the exports and models that read your key tables, so you know who to notify.

reels.title: Matching response to risk and cost

beats.say: Should every bad row stop the whole pipeline? Not always.

Pausing is cheap, but it stops fresh data for everyone. Design for a small blast radius: quarantine the bad partition and let healthy tables flow. Automatic quality gates can halt just the affected branch at three in the morning, before a human wakes.
Backfill has a bill. Rerunning ninety days of a two terabyte table costs real money and can slow other jobs. Run it off peak, in batches, and check each batch.
Match process to severity. A full postmortem for every blip becomes noise, so reserve it for real impact. Track each action item with an owner and a date, or the same failure returns.

show.title: Proportionate process
items: Every action has an owner and date

check.q: What is the main benefit of quarantining a bad partition instead of pausing all pipelines?
opts: It removes the need for a postmortem
It limits the blast radius while healthy data keeps flowing
It makes backfills free
check.why: Quarantine contains the damage to the affected data and avoids stalling everything else, trading a little complexity for freshness.

work: Define severity tiers and what response each one triggers.
Add an automated quality gate on your most critical table.
Review open postmortem action items and assign missing owners.

reels.title: The night nurse for your pipelines

beats.say: What if the first fifteen minutes of every failed data job were already done before you woke up?
Think of a night nurse in a hospital. When an alarm sounds, she does not operate. She checks the chart, takes readings, and writes a note.
Then she wakes the right doctor. An on-call agent works the same way. A pipeline fails and rings the bell. The agent reads the logs, checks the data, and writes a short note with proof.
The note goes to the team that owns the job, looked up from a list, not guessed. And the agent only suggests fixes. A person must approve them.

show.title: Two safety rules
items: Owner is looked up from a list, never guessed
The agent suggests, a person approves

check.q: In the nurse analogy, what does the on-call agent do when a job fails?
opts: Quietly fixes the pipeline on its own
Gathers evidence, writes a note and sends it to the owner
Waits until the next morning for a human to look
check.why: The agent saves the first investigation steps by gathering evidence and reporting. Fixes still need a person's approval.

work: List the last five pipeline failures and note what you checked first each time.
Find out where your team keeps the owner of each pipeline, and whether it is written down.

reels.title: From failed task to Slack message

beats.say: A task fails at three in the morning. What happens in the next thirty seconds?

Airflow retries twice. When the last try fails, a callback posts the dag, task, run, try number, and log link to the agent. A cheap small model classifies the failure, for example bad data, timeout, or schema change.
Next it gathers evidence with tools: read the log, summarize the stage, check table health, trace lineage, search the docs. Then a stronger model writes the diagnosis as a structured plan.
Last, it posts to Slack for the owning team. Cost is about thirty cents per incident at Wix, across thirty five hundred pipelines.

check.q: Why use a small model first and a stronger model later?
opts: Classification is frequent and simple, diagnosis is rarer and harder
The small model is always more accurate
Slack only accepts messages from small models
check.why: Matching model size to the task keeps cost low: the cheap model handles the high volume, the strong one runs only where reasoning is needed.

work: Check that your failure callback fires only after retries are exhausted.
Write down which five read-only tools an agent would need for your pipelines.

reels.title: Evidence or nothing

beats.say: The model wrote a confident root cause. How do you know it is not making it up?
You force the answer into a schema. Summary, root cause, evidence, confidence, next steps, owner, and a needs human flag. Evidence must be exact lines or numbers copied from tool output.

show.title: Diagnosis schema
show.text:
class Diagnosis(BaseModel):
  summary: str
  root_cause: str
  evidence: list[str]
  confidence: Literal[high, medium, low]
  next_steps: list[str]
  owner: str
  needs_human: bool

beats.say: If validation fails, or evidence is empty, the agent posts unknown, here is what I checked. An honest gap beats a confident guess at three in the morning.
The owner field is filled from table metadata, not by the model, because a wrong guess pages the wrong team. And the callback has a five second timeout so the agent can never block Airflow.

chip.text: Routing is a lookup, not a guess

check.q: The model returns a root cause with an empty evidence list. What should the agent do?
opts: Post it anyway with high confidence
Post unknown with what it checked
Retry until the model sounds sure
check.why: A claim not backed by tool output cannot be trusted. Reporting what was checked is honest and still useful to the engineer.

work: Add a rule that rejects any diagnosis whose evidence is empty.
Take the owner from your catalog or metadata, and remove it from the model's output.

reels.title: Proving the agent works

beats.say: How do you know a prompt tweak made the agent better, not just different?
You keep a test set: your eight past incidents with known causes. Replay them after every prompt or tool change and check the root cause matches.
Add healthy runs too, where the right answer is nothing wrong. Without them, an agent that always finds a problem looks perfect.

show.title: Test both sides
items: Real incidents: did it find the cause?
Healthy runs: did it say nothing is wrong?

beats.say: Also log tokens and seconds for every incident. Then you can say what it costs, and whether it saved time.

check.q: Why include healthy runs in the evaluation set?
opts: To make the test set bigger
To catch an agent that invents problems
To lower token cost
check.why: If every test case has a real fault, an agent that always blames something scores well. Healthy runs expose false alarms.

work: Turn your last eight incidents into replayable test cases with the known cause.
Add at least three healthy runs where the expected answer is nothing wrong.

reels.title: Where the agent earns its keep

beats.say: Wix saw twenty eight of one hundred eighty generated fixes merge untouched. Is that a failure?

No. About fifteen percent merging unedited means the agent is a diagnosis tool, not an engineer. Its value is saving the first fifteen minutes of every incident. So keep it read only and send fixes through approval.
Split models by frequency. A small model handles the many simple classifications. The stronger model runs only on real incidents, which keeps cost near thirty cents each.
Do not build this for a handful of pipelines. A runbook and a good alert are cheaper. The agent pays off at scale, with many owners, messy logs, and steady incident volume.

show.title: When it pays off
items: Skip it for a handful of pipelines
Use it with many owners and messy logs

check.q: Only about 15 percent of generated pull requests merged unedited. What is the right design conclusion?
opts: Let the agent merge its own fixes to raise the rate
Drop the agent entirely
Keep it as a read-only diagnoser, with fixes through human approval
check.why: The measured value is faster triage, not autonomous repair. Approval keeps risk low while still saving the first investigation minutes.

work: Estimate incidents per month times cost per incident, and compare it with engineer minutes saved.
Decide whether a runbook plus better alerts would cover most of your incidents before building an agent.

reels.title: Taste before you serve

beats.say: Would a bakery put a cake in the shop window before tasting it?

show.sub: Would you serve an untested cake?

beats.say: A good bakery bakes in the back kitchen, where nobody out front can see. That is the write step. New data lands somewhere private.
Then someone tastes it. That is the audit. Is it sweet enough? Is anything missing? Is it burnt?
Only if it passes does it go in the window. That is publish. If it fails, customers still get yesterday's fresh cake, and the baker gets a warning. Stale but safe beats fresh but wrong.

chip.text: Stale with a warning beats fresh and wrong

check.q: In the bakery story, what happens when the taste test fails?
opts: The cake goes in the window anyway
Customers keep yesterday's cake and the baker is warned
The shop closes for the day
check.why: A failed audit blocks the publish step. Consumers keep the last good data and someone is alerted to fix it.

work: Name one table at work that people read while it is still being loaded.
Ask yourself: if tonight's load were wrong, who would see it first?

reels.title: Three steps, no half-loaded tables

beats.say: How do you load ten million rows without anyone ever seeing half of them?

show.sub: and nobody sees a half-loaded table

beats.say: Step one, write. Load tonight's rows into a staging table called orders staging. Dashboards still read the real orders table, untouched.
Step two, audit. Run checks on staging. Row count within ten percent of yesterday. Order id never null. No duplicate ids. Revenue never negative.

Step three, publish. If every check passes, swap staging in for the live table. In most warehouses a swap only changes metadata, so it takes milliseconds. Readers see old data, then new data, never half.
If any check fails, skip the swap and page someone.

check.q: Why is publishing by swapping tables safe for readers?
opts: The swap copies all rows very quickly
It changes metadata, so readers see old or new data, never half
It locks the table for an hour
check.why: The heavy work happens in staging. The swap only repoints metadata, so it is near instant and all or nothing.

work: Write down three audit checks for your most important table: volume, nulls and duplicates.
Find out whether your warehouse supports an atomic table swap or a view repoint.

reels.title: When the audit lies to you

beats.say: Your audit passed, so why did bad data still reach the dashboard?

show.sub: and the dashboard is still wrong

beats.say: Because an audit only catches what you wrote a test for. Row counts and nulls pass while a currency column quietly doubles. Add checks on value distributions and freshness, not just shape.
Second gotcha: the swap must be atomic. If you drop the old table and then rename the new one, readers hit a gap between the two. Use one swap, a view repoint, or an Iceberg branch fast forward.

show.title: Gap 2: non-atomic swap

beats.say: Third: dbt build only approximates this pattern. It tests a model, then skips the downstream models if the test fails. But the failed model has already been written to its live table.

chip.text: Bad data may already be live in A

check.q: Why can dbt build leave bad data visible even when a test fails?
opts: It never runs tests
The failed model was already written to its live table
It always publishes downstream models first
check.why: dbt builds a model into its real table, then tests it. Only downstream models are skipped, so true write-audit-publish needs a staging step or branch.

work: Check whether your swap or rename is a single atomic statement.
Add one distribution check, such as average order value within a range, to your audits.

reels.title: What write-audit-publish really costs

beats.say: Is write-audit-publish always worth it?
It costs storage and compute. Staging doubles the write for a big table, and a full copy of a ten terabyte table every hour adds up fast.

show.title: Cost of a full staging copy

beats.say: Branching formats like Iceberg make it cheap. A branch only writes new files, and publishing is a metadata fast forward, so there is no second copy.
Skip it for low-stakes, append-only logs where speed matters more. Use it for finance, model training data, and anything feeding other pipelines.
Also decide your failure policy: block, or publish with a warning. Block on money. Warn on a clickstream.

show.sub: Block on money. Warn on clicks.

check.q: Which setup makes write-audit-publish cheapest on a very large table?
opts: Copy the full table into staging every hour
Write to an Iceberg branch and fast forward main after the audit
Skip the audit and rely on alerts
check.why: A branch writes only new files and publishing is a metadata change, so you avoid a second full copy of the table.

work: Rank your tables by blast radius and apply write-audit-publish only to the top tier.
Set a written policy per table: block on failure or publish with a warning.
